entries.title: Germany investigates arms cache found in woods near Berlin last year
entries.summary: Handguns and ammunition were found in a forest near Berlin last year. German authorities suspect they were to be used for assassinations on behalf of Russian intelligence.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany investigates arms cache found in woods near Berlin

August 21, 2026

Handguns and ammunition were found in a forest near Berlin last year. German authorities suspect they were to be used for assassinations on behalf of Russian intelligence.

Security authorities in Germany uncovered a cache of handguns in a forest near the capital Berlin last year, which they believe were intended to be used to carry out assassinations on behalf of Russia, according to reports on Friday.

The daily Süddeutsche Zeitung and public broadcasters NDR and WDR reported that one suspect has been arrested in Romania.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said German authorities were in touch with their Romanian counterparts over the potential extradition of the suspect.

"This case demonstrates that we are ​operating under a high threat level," ​Dobrindt told a press ​conference.

This is a breaking news story and will be updated...

entries.title: Ceuta: Spanish police arrest 5 alleged migrant traffickers
entries.summary: The arrests come after Spain's North African exclave saw a deadly border surge in late July, when tens of thousands of migrants entered Ceuta.
entries.content:
August 21, 2026

The arrests come after Spain's North African exclave saw a deadly border surge in late July, when tens of thousands of migrants entered Ceuta.

Spanish police have arrested five people suspected of charging migrants thousands of euros to bring them from Ceuta, Spain's North African exclave, to mainland Spain.

The arrests come less than a month after the Spanish territory, which borders Morocco, saw a deadly border rush in which over 70,000 migrants entered Ceuta irregularly, with many swimming or crossing on foot.

Dozens of people died in the chaotic scenes. Ceuta's leader Juan Jesus Vivas told EU lawmakers that some 100 people had died, while Spanish NGO Caminando Fronteras said the death toll was 141 people.

The incident renewed debate in Europe on the sensitive issue of migration. Italy temporarily suspended Schengen border-free travel with Spain in response, with Madrid retaliating by imposing border controls on travelers from Italy.

What did Spanish police say about the arrests?

Five people were arrested after two investigations in Ceuta and in La Linea de la Concepcion in Andalusia, which borders British overseas territory Gibraltar.

The suspected traffickers allegedly charged migrants up to €9,000 ($10,500), Spain's Interior Ministry said in a statement, adding that the suspects used small boats "to smuggle migrants from Ceuta to the mainland."

Four of the people arrested are alleged members of a trafficking network that picked up undocumented migrants, sheltered them in houses or garages in Ceuta before smuggling them across the Strait of Gibraltar to Spain.

"Boat drivers were selected for their experience navigating fast and their ability to make evasive manoeuvres and avoid police checks," the statement said.

In one of the crossings, seven people were crammed into an overcrowded dinghy that was barely five meters (16 feet) long and two meters wide for five hours, without life jackets or other adequate safety equipment, police said. The boat ran out of fuel and was left adrift in the Strait of Gibraltar.

Strong currents, changing tides, high winds and heavy maritime traffic combine to make the Strait of Gibraltar extremely dangerous for people attempting to cross it in small boats.

What is the current situation in Ceuta?

Most of the estimated 72,000 migrants who entered Ceuta in late July have returned to Morocco, Spanish officials say. But thousands remain in the enclave, sleeping in makeshift camps, on the street or on the beach.

More than 1,000 migrants were cleared from Trampolin Beach on Friday, after more than 1,200 people were evacuated from the site the day before and moved to shelters.

The Spanish government in Madrid has said it will open temporary centers to ease the burden on Ceuta's overcrowded migrant shelters.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: DRC Ebola outbreak 'growing exponentially,' UN says
entries.summary: The Ebola outbreak in the DRC is rapidly spreading in an area "bigger than France," according to a senior UN official. The WHO is providing the country with thousands of vaccine doses in a bid to contain the virus.
entries.content:
August 21, 2026

The Ebola outbreak in the DRC is rapidly spreading in an area "bigger than France," according to a senior UN official. The WHO is providing the country with thousands of vaccine doses in a bid to contain the virus.

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is "growing exponentially" and risks spilling over into neighboring countries unless containment efforts are stepped up, the UN's senior Ebola coordinator said Friday.

The outbreak is already the deadliest in the country's history, with more than 2,500 deaths from over 5,000 infections.

"The epidemic is spreading widely. It's now covering an area that is bigger than France," UN senior Ebola coordinator Julien Harneis told journalists, adding that half of the 2,500 deaths had been reported in the last 20 days alone.

"It is growing faster and wider than the Ebola response."

He stressed that aid funding and the delivery of resources to remote areas needed to be urgently ramped up to slow and eventually stop the virus's transmission.

"If we do not ... then this epidemic will become more deadly. It will spread wider and it risks to spread into neighboring countries," Harneis added.

Fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak in history

The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare type of Ebola that has no approved vaccine or treatment.

The first infections were detected earlier this year in the DRC's northeastern Ituri province, an area where armed groups operate and health infrastructure is poor. The virus has since spread to five other provinces as well as to neighboring Uganda.

Congolese authorities officially declared an Ebola outbreak on May 15, but experts believe the virus may have already been circulating for some time before that point.

Officials say it is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record and is expanding about three times faster than the 2014-2016 outbreak in West Africa —  the world's deadliest on record— which killed around 11,000 people.

Ebola is spread between people by direct contact with bodily fluids. It can cause fever, fatigue, and muscle pain, followed by vomiting and diarrhea. Some patients also develop internal or external bleeding.

DRC to receive 70,000 doses of Ervebo Ebola vaccine

Meanwhile, the World Health Organization has announced it will immediately release 70,000 doses of Merck's Ervebo Ebola vaccine to the DRC in a bid to help contain the epidemic. 

The Ervebo shot has only been approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, although the WHO said in a statement that early data from animal trials showed it may also give some protection against Bundibugyo — the strain behind the current epidemic.

"The allocation includes 20,000 doses for a Phase 3 clinical trial to understand the impact of the vaccine on the Bundibugyo virus, and 50,000 doses for frontline and health workers," the UN health agency said.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: North Korea: Will Trump-Kim talks happen anytime soon?
entries.summary: As Donald Trump claims a meeting is planned with Kim Jong Un, North Korea's response sends a signal that it wants maximum concessions in return for talks with the US.
entries.content:
North Korea

North Korea: Will Trump-Kim talks happen anytime soon?

August 21, 2026

As Donald Trump claims a meeting is planned with Kim Jong Un, North Korea's response sends a signal that it wants maximum concessions in return for talks with the US.

North Korea responded on Thursday to claims by US President Donald Trump that he will be holding talks with leader Kim Jong Un later in the year with a broadside of ballistic missiles.

The South Korean military said Pyongyang launched 10 short-range missiles that landed in the sea off North Korea's east coast.

This came a day after Kim's powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong, said Pyongyang was "completely unaware of" plans for discussions.

Trump's announcement on Wednesday that he is in contact with Kim and that the two leaders would meet later in the year appears to have caught Pyongyang off guard. It comes after the US president said the military would scale back annual military drills with South Korea.

The statement by Kim Yo Jong, director of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea and one of her brother's closest advisers, dismissed Trump's decision to dramatically scale back the 10-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises as "unworthy of comment and [we] have no interest in it at all."

"After Trump's overtures, Kim Yo Jong effectively said downscaling exercises is not enough, and North Korea launched about a dozen missiles in its third firing in two weeks," Leif-Eric Easley, a professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, told DW.

In a statement carried by the state-run Korea Central News Agency (KCNA), Kim Yo Jong mocked South Korea as a "puppet" and indicated that only canceling the drills in their entirety would be seen as a "goodwill measure."

North Korea's position of power

Choo Jae-woo, a professor of foreign policy at South Korea's Kyung Hee University, told DW that unlike in Trump's first term, Pyongyang right now is in a position of power and will likely seek more guarantees before coming to the negotiating table.

"North Korea is not interested in dialogue because Kim was humiliated in 2019 when Trump walked out of their talks in Hanoi," said Choo said.

Those talks ended in acrimony over the US insistence that North would have to scrap its nuclear program.

Pyongyang has since forged a close security and economic alliance with Russia, granting it access to military technology, energy and consumer goods previously beyond its grasp under international sanctions.

"They are in the safe hands of Russia and China and, in the years since Hanoi, Kim has made it his regime's official position that North Korea will never engage in dialogue as long as giving up its nuclear weapons is part of the discussion,” Choo added.

Will Trump-Kim talks happen anytime soon?

Easley said that Pyongyang is unlikely to agree to talks with the US, at least in the immediate future.

"North Korea is practically a combatant in a European war, sending ammunition, missiles and soldiers to Russia as it continues to attack Ukraine," he said.

"Kim is benefiting financially from this illegal trade, incorporating new technologies and battlefield experience into his military and industrial base, and receiving Moscow's blessing for de facto nuclear status."

That, in turn, gives Kim leverage to demand greater support from Beijing. Pyongyang is also aware that time is not on Trump's side.

Trump has not yet publicly confirmed a date and venue for talks with Kim, and no agenda has been presented, casting doubt on whether a meeting will take place. The upcoming US midterm elections on November 3 add more political urgency to Trump's timeline.

On the other hand, the North Korean leader may sense that this may be his best opportunity to strike some sort of deal with the US while Trump is still in office.

In her statement earlier this week, Kim Yo Jong said the relationship between Trump and her brother is "still excellent."

Seoul welcomes progress

And while the South Korean government has broadly welcomed Trump's claim that he will meet with Kim later in the year and reiterated that it no longer considers denuclearization of the North a prerequisite for talks, there are concerns among ordinary people in the South, Choo said.

"The fear is that Trump will simply ignore South Korea's security needs and deal directly with North Korea because he is so desperate to get an agreement signed," he said.

"There needs to be close coordination between Seoul and Washington on what is being discussed and agreed because any agreements that are made will affect us far more than the US," he said.

Media reports suggest that the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum on November 18 and 19 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen could provide a suitable venue for Trump and Kim to meet in person.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Bauhaus Manifesto: Broad alliance promoting artistic freedom
entries.summary: Weeks before Saxony-Anhalt's state election, representatives from German cultural, crafts, architecture, design and church sectors unite to promote freedom, openness and creativity.
entries.content:
Germany

Bauhaus Manifesto: Broad alliance promoting artistic freedom

August 21, 2026

Weeks before Saxony-Anhalt's state election, representatives from German cultural, crafts, architecture, design and church sectors unite to promote freedom, openness and creativity.

The "Bauhaus Manifesto 2026," published on August 20, was initiated by Germany's Minister of State for Culture, Wolfram Weimer.

"Together, we're making it clear that we want to strengthen the Bauhaus and its principles while defending them against any form of anti-democratic attack," the independent politician told the German press agency DPA.

A statement accompanying the manifesto said it was intended as a cultural and sociopolitical commitment to the principles that have made the Bauhaus art school, which operated from 1919 to 1933, a global cultural icon. Those principles include freedom of artistic thought, openness to new ideas, the connection between different disciplines, and the belief that cultural innovation can make an important contribution to a democratic society.

Something to be proud of

At the publication of the manifesto, Weimer said, "The Bauhaus demonstrates the innovative power that emerges when art, craftsmanship, design and technology converge. It stands for creativity and exchange, courage and openness to new ideas." He said those values remain an important source of inspiration: "We can be proud of that."

The signatories include the German Cultural Council, the German Commission for UNESCO, the German Bishops' Conference, the Evangelical Church in Germany, the Association of German Cities, the German Museums Association, the Academy of Arts, the German Confederation of Skilled Crafts and the German Lost Art Foundation.

The Bauhaus was founded in Weimar in 1919 by architect Walter Gropius and other artists as a school of art and design. It later moved to Dessau and eventually to Berlin. When he founded the school, Gropius outlined its goals in his own "Bauhaus Manifesto." In 1933, the prestigious institution was forced to close permanently under pressure from the Nazis. The Bauhaus and its sites in Weimar, Dessau and Bernau have been UNESCO World Heritage Sites since 1996.

The Bauhaus' international influence is not based solely on its modern design language and avant-garde approach, the new manifesto says. It also stems from its ethos, which remains a model today: the courage to pursue bold ideas, a belief in freedom of artistic thought and the conviction that only an open society can foster cultural renewal.

The signatories also set out to defend the Bauhaus movement itself against populist criticism: "Bauhaus institutions should be strengthened; their creative freedom and social openness recognized as exemplary and they should be defended against any anti-democratic attacks," they say.

A 'misguided aberration of modernity'?

The Alternative for Germany (AFD) party, which has described the Bauhaus as a "misguided aberration of modernity," is not named in the manifesto. But the document can be seen as a response to the far-right party's cultural agenda.

The AfD could emerge as the largest bloc in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament after the September 6 election. The party says it wants to promote a "patriotic cultural policy," primarily supporting art that "contributes to the development of German identity."

The AfD also plans to replace Saxony-Anhalt's current image campaign, #moderndenken (think modern), with #deutschdenken (think German). In its current election manifesto, the party says the Bauhaus has always sought to avoid any hint of "national roots."

The signatories of the "Bauhaus Manifesto 2026" take the opposite view. "We need the sociopolitical impetus of the Bauhaus pioneers precisely at a time when political fringe groups are gaining strength and advocating regression rather than progress," they state.

They also point to the Bauhaus' persecution under the Nazis. "The example of the Bauhaus and the hostility it faced from the Nazi regime reminds us that the culture of remembrance is not a nostalgic look back, but a prerequisite for democratic self-understanding."

The manifesto states that cultural institutions that preserve memory and provide spaces for constructive debate should therefore be supported. The autonomy of artists and cultural institutions, it says, is a fundamental prerequisite for a vibrant democracy.

The Bauhaus is built on the idea of bringing together creative ideas, bold experimentation, high-quality craftsmanship and technological innovation, the manifesto says. It also represents openness and renewal, exchange and networking.

"This openness is a great strength of German culture and enriches Germany," its supporters say. "We reject nationalism that is hostile to culture."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Germany news: Berlin losing its appeal for many Germans
entries.summary: Fewer than a third of Germans find their capital city "fascinating", a sharp fall from 20 years ago, a survey has found. Germany is also mulling further action against Russia over the Leipzig drone incident. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Berlin losing its appeal for many Germans

Published August 21, 2026last updated August 21, 2026

Fewer than a third of Germans find their capital city "fascinating", a sharp fall from 20 years ago, a survey has found. Germany is also mulling further action against Russia over the Leipzig drone incident. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • More Germans think Berlin 'lacks charisma' than those who find it 'fascinating,' according to a survey
  • Panda twins Leni and Lotti celebrate their second birthday at Berlin Zoo
  • The German government is reportedly considering sanctioning a Russian cultural center in the capital over the recent drone incident at Leipzig airport
  • Nearly a quarter of German companies are facing a shortage of skilled workers

This is a roundup of the stories making headlines in Germany on Friday, August 21 2026:

Skip next section At least 8 injured after car crashes into storefront in Hesse

At least 8 injured after car crashes into storefront in Hesse

At least eight people sustained minor injuries after a car appeared to lose control and hit people in a pedestrian-only section in Hofgeismar in the central German state of Hesse.

Police cited witnesses as saying that the driver of the car appeared to have been experiencing medical difficulties right before the incident unfolded.

Locals noticed the man behind the wheel at a crosswalk and approached him to help, but he sped into the pedestrian zone and hit several people.

His car ultimately came to a stop after he crashed into a storefront.

Other passersby immediately offered help to the driver, who has now been taken to hospital, where his condition is reportedly critical, according to police.

The accident site remains cordoned off.

Skip next section Berlin weighing sanctions against Russian cultural center over Leipzig drone incident

Berlin weighing sanctions against Russian cultural center over Leipzig drone incident

Amid mounting evidence that Russia was behind the planned drone attack on Leipzig Airport this month, the German government is reportedly considering imposing sanctions on the controversial Russian House cultural center in Berlin.

German government officials have avoided publicly blaming Moscow for the incident, in which an explosive-laden drone was found at the airport in Leipzig.

But according to Der Spiegel, Berlin is weighing possible sanctions against Russia, including targeting the Russian House on Friedrichstrasse.

Moscow says it is a cultural center, but security officials in Germany suspect it is also used for espionage activities.

Despite the frosty ties between Berlin and Moscow in recent years, Germany has resisted closing the center for fear that Russia would retaliate by closing Goethe Institutes in Moscow and St. Petersburg — the last remaining representations of German civil society in Russia.

Skip next section Almost 1/4 of German companies face shortage of skilled workers

Almost 1/4 of German companies face shortage of skilled workers

Nearly one in four companies in Germany are facing a lack of skilled workers, the Munich-based ifo institute said Friday.

The survey found that 23.2% of German firms had reported a shortage of skilled staff in July, a 2-point increase since April.

The long-term average of German companies reporting skilled labor shortages remains much higher, at 31.7%.

A "weak economy" is currently limiting demand for skilled workers, ifo researcher Daria Schaller said.

But she warned that as Germany's economy recovers, "the shortage of skilled workers is likely to increase considerably again."

Demand rose most sharply in the telecommunications sector, where 31.1% of firms were lacking skilled workers, compared to 16.3% in April.

Nearly 65% of companies in the consultancy and auditing sectors were facing skilled labor shortages, up from 52.4%.

Skip next section Germany's gas stores at 'historic low' for time of year

Germany's gas stores at 'historic low' for time of year

Gas storage facilities in Germany are less full for the time of year than at any point since 2011, when records began.

"The current gas storage level is by far the lowest ever recorded for this time of year in Germany," Sebastian Heinermann, INES managing director told German news agency dpa. "It is therefore a historic low."

Find out why Germany's gas storage levels are so low in this in-depth report by DW's Nik Martin. 

Skip next section Panda twins celebrate second birthday at Berlin Zoo

Panda twins celebrate second birthday at Berlin Zoo

Berlin Zoo held a birthday party for two of its most popular residents: twin pandas Leni and Lotti, who are turning two years old this weekend.

The panda cubs were treated to a special ice cake made of beetroot and carrot juice, which was waiting for them on the climbing frame in their outdoor enclosure, Berlin Zoo said in a statement.

"The two panda twins devoured the icy birthday surprise with obvious enthusiasm," the zoo said.

Born on August 22, 2024, the sisters have grown from tiny cubs weighing less than 170 grams (under 6 ounces) each into giant pandas. Leni weighs more than 70 kilograms (154 pounds), while Lotti weighs around 61 kilograms.

"Two years ago, Leni and Lotti could still fit in our hands; today, together they weigh more than 130 kilograms. Watching them develop is very special for our entire team. As true Berliners, they have long since found many fans in the city," said Zoo and Animal Park Director Dr. Andreas Knieriem.

The pandas' names have a special connection to Berlin: Leni is named after iconic German actress and Berlin native Marlene Dietrich, while Lotti is named after Charlottenburg, which neighbors the zoo.

Their mother Meng Meng arrived in Germany in 2017 as part of an agreement with China, which has gifted pandas to friendly nations as part of its "panda diplomacy" policy.

China maintains ownership of the animals and any cubs that are produced, and virtually all cubs born outside China are eventually returned.

Knieriem said Leni and Lotti are "ambassadors for a species whose protection can only succeed through international cooperation. Because we mustn't forget that fewer than 2,000 giant pandas live in their natural habitat."

The giant panda is listed as "vulnerable" to extinction by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

Skip next section Berlin not as appealing to Germans today compared to 20 years ago — survey

Berlin not as appealing to Germans today compared to 20 years ago — survey

A new survey has found that Berlin is losing its appeal to many Germans.

An Allensbach Institute poll published by the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) on Friday found that 31% of respondents consider their capital city to be a "fascinating metropolis."

The same survey found that 36% of the 1,039 people polled think Berlin lacks charisma.

The figures represent a sharp decline in Berlin's appeal among Germans. A previous Allensbach survey from 2007 showed that 66% thought the capital was "fascinating," with only 14% saying it lacked appeal.

Famously described by former mayor Klaus Wowereit as "poor but sexy," Berlin has seen tens of thousands of workers move to the city, causing rents to soar.

This has in turn placed increasing strain on world-famous Berlin's nightclubs, many of which are being priced out by property developers.

Hamburg (48%) and Munich (47%) lead the way for Germans who were asked which cities are particularly appealing.

Asked which cities they would not want to live in, Berlin scored 46%, making it the least popular city alongside financial capital Frankfurt am Main.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen! from Bonn, where the long-overdue rain from the past two days has eased ahead of the weekend.

We begin our coverage of Germany today with the news that Berlin, widely considered one of the world's coolest cities for its vibrant cultural and nightlife scenes, is losing its appeal to many Germans.

Boosting the German capital's appeal — at least for today — is the second birthday celebration of panda twins Leni and Lotti at Berlin Zoo.

In other news from Berlin, the federal government is considering sanctioning a long-standing Russian cultural center in the capital over the recent explosive-laden drone that was found at Leipzig Airport this month.

Bleibt dran as we bring you more on these headlines and plenty more besides.

entries.title: Ronaldinho to make football comeback aged 46
entries.summary: More than a decade after his last professional appearance, Brazilian superstar Ronaldinho is set for a comeback. The former world player of the year is to play in Italy’s third tier.
entries.content:
Brazil

Ronaldinho to make football comeback aged 46

August 21, 2026

More than a decade after his last professional appearance, Brazilian superstar Ronaldinho is set for a comeback. The former world player of the year is to play in Italy’s third tier.

While Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo are still playing at 39 and 41 respectively, most football fans thought Ronaldinho belonged to another footballing era.

That all changed in June, when Italian Serie C club, Ravenna, announced that the former Barcelona, Paris Saint-Germain and AC Milan forward would play for them in the upcoming season.

On a rainy Thursday in northeastern Italy, the former Ballon d'Or winner was unveiled with a quick press conference and a sense of excitement gripping the city.

"I'm very happy to be here with friends, we have a team that can do something good," said Ronaldinho.

"I just arrived, but I have a great desire to live this experience with the whole city."

Pure PR?

The 46-year-old last played for Fluminense in his homeland in 2015 and will become a shareholder in Ravenna, owned by Ignazio Cipriani, an Italian-American businessman who has owned the club since 2024.

Despite holding up the shirt and signing a piece of paper for the cameras, the suspicion remains that this is little more than a PR stunt for an ambitious lower league club. Ronaldinho himself didn't actually dispel those rumors.

"Will you see me play? I don't know, only the coach knows that," he said. "Coming back to Italy is wonderful, I'm here to help my teammates win."

Both the Brazilian and Cipriani used the same language to describe one of Ronaldinho's motivations: "Friendship and passion," they both said. Both men also referred to Ronaldinho's quest to score a 300th professional goal.

"His objective is romantic, to try to score his last goal," Cipriani said.

"His involvement is not a token gesture or a marketing stunt to get people talking about us."

The way in which that figure has been reached is slightly unclear, with many widely used resources saying Ronaldinho has scored far fewer than 299 goals in his career. He has, however, won the Ballon d'Or in 2005, the 2002 World Cup and topflight titles in Spain and Italy.

Ronaldinho some way off Japan's Miura

Whether he ends up playing or not, Ronaldinho's presence in the northeastern city of about 160,000 inhabitants has sparked plenty of anticipation and ticket sales. Reports suggest the club has sold 2,700 season tickets, largely off the back of the Brazilian's arrival.

Even if he does get onto the pitch at 46, Ronaldinho will be far from the oldest footballer around. That title has long belonged to Japan's Kazuyoshi Miura, 59.

The former Japan international, who also played in Italy, scored two penalties in the country's Emperor's Cup competition this week, further extending his record as the world's oldest player.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Why is Israel's military presence growing in Syria?
entries.summary: The recent Israeli attack on a Syrian airbase is just one of many Israeli incursions into Syria. In southern Syria, locals say Israeli troops have detained them, destroyed infrastructure and set up military bases.
entries.content:
Syria

Why is Israel's military presence growing in Syria?

August 21, 2026

The recent Israeli attack on a Syrian airbase is just one of many Israeli incursions into Syria. In southern Syria, locals say Israeli troops have detained them, destroyed infrastructure and set up military bases.

It's been two years, four months, 24 days and five hours, said Syrian man Ahmad Hassan al-Din when asked how long it's been since he last saw his son.

In April 2024, Israeli soldiers took Saddam, who had just turned 17, from farmland near the Golan Heights, a part of Syria Israel has occupied since 1967.

"Saddam had gone to feed the animals early in the morning," al-Din, who's from the village of Jubata al-Khashab in the Quneitra district near Golan, told DW. "I called him on the phone, and he told me, 'Everything's fine.' But then later we saw with our own eyes how they took the boy, handcuffed and shackled."

Al-Din filmed Israeli soldiers marching his son through fields. The video, which he forwarded to DW, has previously been verified by open-source investigators at France24 and by human rights organizations.

"They said they took him because he was trespassing on the territory of the state of Israel," al-Din continued. "Even though that area is our farmland and we have a valid UN permit to work there."

To enter this buffer area, Syrian farmers and shepherds needed a special pass from the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force, or UNDOF. The latter was set up to make sure Israeli and Syrian forces kept their distance after a 1974 disengagement agreement.

Humanitarian organizations have since discovered Saddam, now 19, is likely in a prison in Israel.

DW asked the Israeli military what Saddam had been charged with and under which legal system. A spokesperson sent DW a statement similar to one previously sent to other media outlets and human rights organizations that said Israel detains Syrians that it suspects might wish it harm. The statement did not specify whether the army considered the farmer's son to be one of those individuals.

Israel takes over buffer zone

Since Saddam was taken, the Syrian teenager's story has become one of many similar accounts in this part of southern Syria.

After the fall of the country's dictatorial Assad regime in December 2024, Israel took control of the UN-patrolled demilitarized zone. Senior Israeli politicians declared the 1974 agreement void and said troops would be in the area temporarily to protect Israel from cross-border attacks.

However, since then Israel's presence in Syria has become more permanent. In November 2025, UNDOF told reporters Israel had set up 10 bases in the area. From these bases, Israeli soldiers are making near-daily incursions into the Syrian provinces of Daraa and Quneitra.

"These incursions typically involve armored patrols through populated areas, followed by the establishment of temporary checkpoints on main roads, where all passing Syrian civilians are stopped, searched, questioned, and have their phones examined. In some cases, biometric data is also collected," Syrian consultancy, Karam Shaar Advisory, wrote in January.

Israeli soldiers have also raided homes, businesses and schools and fenced off farmland and water sources.

Quneitra authorities sent DW a statement claiming Israeli troops had seized more than 200 sheep, destroyed drinking water wells, razed horticultural areas and destroyed buildings.

Mousa Khalil, a resident of Quneitra, recounted how his home, a two-story building with four apartments in Hamidiyah village, was completely destroyed by Israeli troops last year.

"I am 65 years old," he told DW. "At this age, finding decent work has become extremely difficult, forcing me to accept whatever I can find to provide for my family of eight and to save money to rebuild our home."

Increased Israel incursions

Over the past few months, the number of these kinds of incursions has been rising, and Israeli soldiers have also been moving farther inside Syria.

The Sijil Center, based in Syria, documents Israeli violations of Syrian territory. Between August 25 and December 31, 2025, the center recorded 818 incidents, or 45 incidents per week. Since the beginning of this year, the center has counted 1,632 incursions, bringing the average to 48 incidents weekly.

The Sijil Center also documents how many Syrians have been detained by Israel and says that, since December 2024, around 200 people have been apprehended. Unlike al-Din's son, most were released within 24 hours after being interrogated.

Between 40 and 50 Syrians are thought to remain in Israeli jails, including four or five who were in custody before the change of Syrian government in 2024.

Soldiers coming across a border and detaining citizens of another country, then transferring them back to their own prisons, is clearly a breach of international law, experts say. Organizations like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have described Israel's actions in southern Syria as possible war crimes.

Why is Israel doing this?

Since the fall of the previous Syrian government, Israeli politicians have insisted that southern Syria must be a "demilitarized zone."

The Israeli military previously told other news outlets that it has "apprehended individuals where there was reasonable suspicion of their involvement in terrorist activity." The army also acknowledged the construction of new military bases to prevent attacks and smuggling.

"The area is a playground for terror organizations, armed groups and militias," a senior officer told Israel's Ynet last week. 

Speaking to media outlet Syria Direct, locals in Quneitra said they weren't sure whether Israel is trying to occupy their towns, or whether it is doing this to pressure the Syrian government.

Senior Syrian and Israeli politicians had been involved in talks, with mediation from the US, to potentially reactivate the 1974 disengagement agreement. But talks fell apart late in 2025 and in the intervening months, Israeli incursions into Syria increased.

In an analysis this week, Elizabeth Tsurkov, a senior non-resident fellow at the Washington-based New Lines Institute, outlined reasons for Israel's behavior in Syria.

"The first factor that drives Israel's Syria approach is the collective trauma of October 7th, which left the Israeli public and security establishment fearing a repeated cross-border invasion," she explained. Other motives include Israel's assumption that the new Syrian government is hostile, even though it has continuously said it doesn't want to fight and has not launched any attacks.

"Because Israel reads the government in Damascus as jihadist and subservient to Turkey, its overarching goal is a central government too weak to threaten it," Tsurkov wrote.

On Tuesday night this week, Israeli jets bombed the Abu Duhur military air base in northern Syria shortly after a Turkish delegation had visited it. Senior Israeli politicians have recently predicted their next war could be with Syria or Turkey.

Following the attack on the airbase Syria's Foreign Minister was interviewed by US news outlet Axios. He said that during year-long negotiations on a security deal, significant progress was made but Israel walked away.

"Security cannot be one-sided," he said, noting that Syria was open to further talks. "Just as we take Israeli security concerns into account, Israel must also take Syrian security concerns into account and seriously address our concerns regarding its expansionist policy and military operations inside Syrian territory."

In a recent study, Syrian think tank Etana came up with some other reasons for Israel's actions in Syria. Israeli control of Syria's tallest peak, Mount Hermon, also allows Israel to surveil Lebanon, researchers noted.

Water security could also play a part, they suggested. "After its post-Assad intervention in Syria, Israel now has direct control of, or indirect access to, most of the areas rich in surface water resources in Quneitra and western Daraa," they wrote.

What happens next?

Recent history shows that Israeli security zones often turn into permanently occupied or annexed territories, said H.A. Hellyer, a senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London.

Locals like Khalil from Hamidiyah have complained that their own government isn't helping them.

But in fact, in the face of Israel's military superiority, the Syrians are probably doing the best they can, Hellyer told DW. "They're continuing on the diplomatic track because they know very well that they have no military option here," he said.

"All this is part and parcel of what I would describe as Israeli paramountcy," Hellyer added, referring to a concept that describes how powerful states override weaker ones by sheer force of arms. "It basically means they are paramount. They have the ability to do what they want. Nobody has the ability to say no, and laws and rules are out the window, without any consensus building at all," he concluded.

This article was originally published August 20, 2026, updated on August 21, 2026, to include a response from the Israeli military.

Edited by: Martin Kuebler

entries.title: Panama Canal to cap ship transits due to El Nino drought
entries.summary: Panama Canal will cut daily transits of ships from September because of low rainfall and amid an intensifying El Nino event.
entries.content:
August 21, 2026

Panama Canal will cut daily transits of ships from September because of low rainfall and amid an intensifying El Nino event.

The Panama Canal will cut the number of ships passing through it starting next month due to a lack of rainfall as the El Nino weather pattern takes hold over the region, the canal operator said on Thursday.

The vital waterway across Panama in Central America links the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. About 5% of global maritime trade uses it, cutting thousands of kilometers off journeys and avoiding a dangerous route around the southern tip of Argentina.

From September 3, the waterway will allow 34 ships to pass through it, instead of the current 36, the Panama Canal Authority said.

From September 15, the number of ships allowed to pass through it will drop to 32.

That Panama is experiencing severe drought even though it is one of the wettest nations on Earth is a sign that El Nino has formed in a warmed-up Pacific Ocean. Rainfall between May and August was about 34% below the historical average for the period, the canal operator said.

What is El Nino?

El Nino is characterized by unusually warm ocean surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific, with knock-on effects including droughts, floods and wildfires.

Those changes in winds and ocean temperatures will likely turbocharge extreme weather events because of how warm the world already is from fossil fuel pollution, experts say.

Scientists say they expect El Nino to get so intense this late fall and early winter that "it would rank among the largest El Nino events in the historical record going back to 1950."

Panama Canal affected by drought in recent years

The 50-mile (80-kilometer) Panama Canal was impacted by severe drought in 2023-2024, when the canal operator slashed ship crossings.

In 2023, the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low the waterway's operators cut the daily ship transit number from 38 to 22.

The authority has already implemented water conservation measures but called for methods to bolster the "long-term sustainability" of the waterway.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Alaska charter flight crash kills 8
entries.summary: A small ‌Cessna 441 plane operated by a private charter company crashed near a US military-managed radar site in Alaska. All on board have reportedly died.
entries.content:
United States of America

Alaska charter flight crash kills 8

August 21, 2026

A small ‌Cessna 441 plane operated by a private charter company crashed near a US military-managed radar site in Alaska. All on board have reportedly died.

A charter plane crash at a remote military radar site in western Alaska on Thursday has left all eight people on board dead, according to the United States  military.

The aircraft  crashed around 12:15 pm (2015 UTC) on approach to Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, located about 725 kilometers (450 miles) west of Anchorage, Alaska's largest city, from where it had departed.

Six passengers and two pilots were aboard the plane during the incident, said Clint Johnson, Alaska region chief of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB).

Reports identified the plane as a ‌Cessna 441 operated by Anchorage-based air charter company Security Aviation.

Alaska Senator Lisa Murkowski expressed her condolences, following news of the crash.

"I've traveled extensively with Security Aviation throughout Alaska, and have met many of their experienced pilots," she said on X, naming the charter company that operates in the remote region.

She added that multiple agencies, including the US Coast Guard, NTSB, Alaska State Troopers, and the Rescue Coordination Center had responded to the crash.

Air Force Alaskan Command mourns 'loss for our military family'

The Associated Press cited the US ​military's Alaskan Command as saying that the plane was a "civilian-contracted aircraft."

The passengers on board were "dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment," AP quoted Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, commander of Alaskan Command, the Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region and Eleventh Air Force, as saying in a statement.

The specifics of what work the crash victims were doing at the radar site — which tracks aircraft operating in Alaskan airspace — was not immediately clear from the Alaskan Command's statement.

"This is a devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve," Davis said, according to AP.

The Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center manages the radar site.

Edited by: Zac Crellin
